We maintain a transparent approach in showing revisions to UK gross domestic product (GDP) estimates by publishing real-time estimates of GDP, alongside our data vintages, and by providing a timely assessment of these revisions.

There is a mean revision between the first estimate and the final estimate of positive 0.1 percentage points over the period Quarter 1 (Jan to Mar) 1961 to Quarter 4 (Oct to Dec) 2023; for the period Quarter 1 2020 to Quarter 4 2023, there is a mean revision of positive 0.3 percentage points, which includes the impact of the uncertainty around the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

When we look at the sign of quarterly GDP growth, of the 175 times where the growth in the first estimate was positive, 168 of these (96%) have remained positive in the final estimate, while 42 of the 64 (66%) instances where the growth in the first estimate was negative have remained negative.
For the period between May 2018 and December 2023, the mean revision to the first estimate of the three-month change in GDP is positive 0.26 percentage points.

in the annual production round, with a time series that goes back to 1948 annually and 1955 quarterly. In the UK, we produce a first estimate of quarterly GDP six weeks after that quarter ends, alongside our higher-frequency monthly GDP estimates, which are also available around 40 days after the month ends.

There is a trade-off between the timeliness and accuracy of estimates of GDP. As additional information becomes available, we have a more complete picture of economic activity in that period. the relative mean absolute revision (RMAR), which incorporates the size of the initial estimate in relation to the revision, as a large revision on a very large initial growth rate can have less of an impact than a large revision to a very small initial growth rate

For example, the Blue Book 2026 revisions reflect those between the August 2026 and September 2026 vintages of quarterly estimates of volume GDP – this includes up to Quarter 2 (Apr to June) 2026.

We also introduce major methodological improvements during the annual Blue Book process to ensure that changes are implemented in a consistent and coordinated way. These changes can take place beyond the three-year production cycle. Our

This looks at the revisions in each Blue Book and relates to the period from Quarter 1 (Jan to Mar) 1997 to the latest quarter available in that publication that was open to revision. It is one indicator of the trade-off between timeliness and accuracy, and also captures methodological improvements that come through our annual Blue Books.

The main methodological and data improvements in Blue Book 2026 are the incorporation of the Annual Survey of Goods and Services (ASGS), which gives us more information on products that are produced by the services industries, and changes to our estimates of actual and imputed rentals. For quarterly changes in volume GDP, the MAR for Blue Book 2026 was 0.04 percentage points.

There will be some periods where revisions are larger, where this likely reflects higher levels of uncertainty in early estimates (for example, the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic) and/or where methodological and data changes have had more pronounced impacts in specific years. This can help to show what drives larger revisions to gross domestic product (GDP).

Two examples of years that have seen larger annual GDP revisions over a number of subsequent Blue Books are 2012 and 2017. In this section, we explore how the level of GDP has been revised up in these years because of methodological and data improvements across subsequent Blue Books.
